questions.stem: Which bonds make addition polymers so unreactive?

options.text: Strong carbon-carbon bonds throughout the chain
options.explanation: The joining up of monomers leaves a backbone that ordinary chemistry struggles to attack.
Intermolecular forces decide melting, not chemical inertness of the chain itself.
The polymer chain is covalent; no ionic bonding holds it together.

options.text: Open double bonds left all along the chain
options.explanation: Addition polymerisation consumes the double bonds as the chain forms.

questions.stem: What does it mean to describe an addition polymer as inert?

options.explanation: Inert means the substance resists chemical attack, which is why it persists.
Radioactivity has nothing to do with the disposal problem here.
Flammability is a separate hazard discussed under incineration.
Magnetism is irrelevant to polymer chemistry.

questions.stem: Why can decomposers not break addition polymers down?

options.text: The polymers are non-biodegradable because their strong bonds resist attack
options.explanation: Inertness blocks the microbial chemistry that biodegradation depends on.

options.text: Decomposers simply refuse to eat plastic
options.explanation: Preference is not the mechanism; the bonds resist the chemistry.

options.text: Landfill sites are too cold for any life
options.explanation: Life thrives in landfill; the polymer itself is the obstacle.

options.text: The polymer molecules are too small to see
options.explanation: Visibility is irrelevant; molecules are always invisible.

questions.stem: Which statement about landfill disposal of polymers is correct?

options.text: Sites fill up quickly because the buried polymer never breaks down
options.explanation: Permanent burial consumes space that natural decay would eventually free.

options.text: Polymers dissolve into the soil over time
options.explanation: Inert polymers neither dissolve nor decay in the soil.

options.text: Polymers evaporate from the site within years
options.explanation: Solid polymers do not evaporate at landfill temperatures.

options.text: Landfill naturally turns polymers into compost
options.explanation: Composting requires biodegradable material, which these polymers are not.

questions.stem: Which phrase correctly describes the biodegradability of addition polymers?

options.explanation: The spec lists their inability to biodegrade as a named disposal problem.

options.text: They biodegrade within a few months
options.explanation: That describes natural materials, not addition polymers.

options.text: They biodegrade only in strong sunlight
options.explanation: Sunlight may weather surfaces but the spec does not grant biodegradation.

options.text: They biodegrade once buried and wet
options.explanation: Moisture does not unlock the strong carbon backbone.

questions.stem: Which greenhouse gas does burning polymers release?

options.explanation: The combustion of the carbon backbone releases it, contributing to climate change.
That gas is toxic rather than a greenhouse gas, and needs chlorine in the polymer.
Monoxide comes from incomplete burning and is toxic, not a greenhouse driver.
Methane is not listed among the combustion products here.

questions.stem: Which polymer releases toxic hydrogen chloride when burned?

options.explanation: Chlorine in the chain leaves as hydrogen chloride gas on burning.

options.text: Polyethene, which contains only carbon and hydrogen
options.explanation: Without chlorine there is nothing to make hydrogen chloride.
Its hydroxyl groups do not supply chlorine either.
Polyesters carry oxygen but no chlorine, so no hydrogen chloride forms.

questions.stem: Which gas forms when incineration is incomplete?

options.explanation: Limited oxygen supply leaves carbon only partly oxidised, producing the toxic gas.
The dioxide is the complete-combustion product; incompleteness gives the monoxide.
That gas tracks chlorine content, not oxygen supply.
Steam forms whenever hydrogen burns and is not the toxic concern.

questions.stem: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to people?

options.text: It reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen
options.explanation: The gas binds where oxygen should travel, quietly starving the body of it.

options.text: It burns the skin on contact
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide is a gas breathed in; skin burning is not its harm.
It is toxic without any explosive behaviour.
Solvent action on plastics is irrelevant to its toxicity.

questions.stem: Which benefit keeps incineration in use despite its hazards?

options.text: Polymers release a lot of heat energy when they burn
options.explanation: That heat can be recovered, which is why burning remains in the disposal mix.
Burning destroys the polymer; it never improves biodegradability.

options.text: Incineration produces no gases at all
options.explanation: The method is precisely the source of several hazardous gases.

options.text: Incineration needs no fuel to run
options.explanation: The polymer itself burns, but the claim of needing no fuel misses the point.
